items.text: Baan Noi charges you about $22 a person, which I think is fair for the meal. The pad see ew is what you order. The noodles actually taste like something, good texture, and it's a good dish. However, the green curry is way too sweet, too much sugar. So it's not the meal that put me off, but the service. We went on a Friday and waited a long time, and the kitchen was clearly struggling. So you get a decent meal, but you have to deal with the service. I really wanted to like it. But I could get the same thing somewhere else in town. And the good stuff, the good stuff is too easy to get at the bad. So I'd rather go somewhere that gets both right.

We wanted O, but it was on hiatus, so we booked La Rêve. We were staying at Encore, so the theater was a short walk away. Our seats were about the third row. I knew it gets compared to O, even called derivative, so I figured it was a fair substitute. It isn't O, but it's solid.

I don't know, maybe it has a story, but I didn't really get it. Not really a problem for me. Pre-show, a funny lizard guy swims in the pool, just sits there, still, looks like a statue. Then he sneaks up on the front rows and sprays them.

Then the main event, the draw. Pool with platforms that rise and lower. Swimmers, divers, walking on water. From about 25 feet above, this dive. So if you want a good Vegas show, not as expensive as Cirque du Soleil, La Rêve is a good alternative. We liked it. We were impressed.

A pool with platforms that rise and lower, people swimming and diving and walking on water. And diving from a huge height, maybe 25 feet above the pool. If you want to see a big impressive Vegas show but not the very high prices of Cirque du Soleil, I think La Rêve is a good alternative. We left very impressed.

A rain gauge works by catching rainwater in a circular opening. This water drains into a tube with a scale, showing you the depth of rain as if it spread evenly across the ground, not absorbed or run off. Usually, the top opening is bigger than the measuring tube. Narrowing it down, the amount of water is concentrated so small amounts are easier to read. The scale accounts for the difference in area, so the reading is the actual rainfall depth.

Readings are not always accurate. Where the gauge is positioned matters. Near trees, buildings or fences, it can collect more or less, because of sheltering or splashing. Also, if you do not read the gauge soon after a storm, some water will evaporate.

A rain gauge is a simple tool. Rain drops through a circular opening of known area into a measuring tube marked in millimeters or inches. The reading gives the rainfall depth, as if the rain had spread evenly on ground without water being absorbed or running off. The opening is usually larger than the tube to concentrate the water, so you can read smaller amounts better. This is why the scale is corrected to compensate for the area difference. And the gauge placement matters. Near trees, buildings or fences, it will collect too little or too much. If you don't read the water soon after the storm, some of it evaporates. So, it's important to read it quickly.

A rain gauge is basic. You place a funnel to catch the rain, and then measure the depth of the water. The opening is wider than the measuring tube. That's why the scale on the tube is different than it would be on a larger tube. The depth of the water tells you how deep the rain would have been if it had fallen evenly on the ground with no runoff or soaking in. The opening is wider than the tube, so it concentrates the water into a narrow column, making small amounts of rain easier to read accurately. Common issues with rain gauges are bad placement and evaporation. If your gauge is near a tree, a building, or a fence, it may get too little or too much rain because of sheltering or splashing. So if you don't read it right after the storm, you'll get a slightly lower reading because some water evaporates.

She found it where she always does, in the kitchen on Thursday mornings. It was jammed between the flour bins and the cooling racks, just wedged into that little wall cavity. The spine is cracked, there's a faded library stamp on the inside cover, and the due date is long gone.

That's 11 Thursdays now. She's asked the day shift, checked the locks. Stayed here with a thermos and a rolling pin. Once. Nothing. That's just what happens. It appears between 2 and 4 a.m. She never catches it.

Tonight it's heavier. She opened it and a folded receipt paper came out.

"I keep meaning to bring it back to the library. But I walk past your window on the way, and the light is on. And I think, somebody's awake. And so I leave it here instead. Sorry. I'll stop if you ask me to."

She read it twice. The ovens were ticking behind her, first trays of rye waiting under their cloths. She turned the receipt over, found a pencil stub behind her ear, wrote on the back, "Don't stop." Tucked it back in the cover, set it on the sill by the front window. And left the light on.

Arthur woke at 2:40 a.m. because the sour tang of fermenting rye overtook the smell of floor bleach. He wiped his palms on his jeans and reached behind the wicker bannetons. Resting on the bottom wire rack was the library's taped-up copy of The Count of Monte Cristo. It was the fourth Thursday. The spine ran flush with the steel edge. He pulled it free. Stuck to the cover was a square of blue prescription notepad, written in ballpoint ink that had pressed through the paper. It said: The baker in chapter five reminds me of you. Thank you for keeping the lights on. His thumb traced the deep indentation of the pen strokes. The only sound was the shudder of the compressor. A slip of paper drifted down from the back of the book, a yellowing due-date card stamped in faded red ink, three days overdue. He walked to the prep table, wrapped a warm, glaze-mapped cinnamon roll in parchment paper and slipped it into his coat pocket alongside the book.

I paid $38. Kept it because of the switches. Asked the seller what switches and took a week to reply. By then I took off a key cap to find out myself. Brown tactile switches. Small bump under the finger. Soft landing at the bottom. Old membrane board felt like pushing in wet cardboard.

I booked Turkish Airlines. Harbin-Beijing domestic, then Beijing-Istanbul. Harbin leg was delayed, missed connection. At the Turkish booth nobody took responsibility or helped rebook me. Slept at airport. Next morning asked for a ticket. Said flights overbooked, could take days to get me to Istanbul unless I paid business class. Had to get there so accepted it. Still furious, honestly in disbelief.

I'm writing a warning for Turkish Airlines. I booked a domestic flight from Harbin to Beijing and a Turkish flight from Beijing to Istanbul. The Harbin flight was delayed, so I missed the connection. At the Turkish booth, nobody helped me rebook. I just slept in the airport. Next morning I asked for a ticket. They said flights were overbooked, and I could wait days for a flight to Istanbul unless I pay for business class. I needed to be there, so I agreed. I'm still furious and in total shock.

I'm warning you if you fly with Turkish Airlines. I was domestic Harbin to Beijing and then Beijing to Istanbul. Because of delays, missed my flight. They didn't help. They didn't rebook me. I slept at airport. Next morning, asked for ticket. They said flights are overbooked, they will get me to Istanbul in a couple of days unless I pay for business class. But I had to get to Istanbul, so I took it. Still angry. In disbelief, honestly, at Turkish.

The crate was just a milk crate sitting by the back door. Imre found a book in it every Thursday around 2pm. First week it was this field guide to mushrooms from the Carver Street library, due date long gone. Next two weeks, same book. He didn't try to put it back anymore. Just left it on the flour bench next to the scale and the rye starter. It was soft and dusty with thumbprints.

Tonight he nudged the crate with his hip and the book was there again, heavier than it should be. A yellow piece of paper was sticking out near page 112. He took off his oven mitts. The note was written in small, slanted-to-right pencil. It said: "Your door smells better than the library. I keep meaning to bring it to the right place. Is the morel on this page the one you use? —T."

He looked at the page. The morel was there, brown and wrinkled. No circle around it. He got the pencil behind his ear, flipped the note over and wrote: No, never used one. Then, after a beat: Come at five, there's bread. He put it back in the book.

It was past three in the morning, 3:17 to be exact. Marisol heard the walk-in cooler kick on and the proofing cabinet breathe. She put the first loaves into the oven. By the back door was a basket that held a book. It was the same worn paperback again, The Borrowers. The cover was faded. For six Thursdays, somebody had left it there, the library two blocks over. The checkout card in back was blank, only a barcode and a coffee ring marked it. She wiped her hands on her apron, and read the note. The note was tucked between 84 and 85. It said "I can't get to the library before it closes. Please keep it here another week. I like knowing it's warm." She looked at the basket, then the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the roll with the most icing, wrapped it in wax paper, and tucked the note back into the book. She set both by the door. At 4:50, she pulled the loaves, knocked them from their pans, and slid the next tray into the oven.

I paid $38 for this used mechanical keyboard. I just wanted a keyboard with all keycaps, no gunk, and switches that did not feel like typing on gravel. On that scale it did fine. It arrived clean enough to put on my desk without a deep cleaning project, keys have a nice weight to them. I type long emails, and this is actually comfortable for it. Fingers don't feel abused after long typing stretches. More than I can say for some newer cheap keyboards.

Rough edges are there. Space bar rattles when I catch it off center, little loose clack makes the whole board sound more flimsy than it feels. One key will repeat, then not, so I look up and there's an extra letter in the middle of a sentence. Not constant, but annoying.

Comms were also poor. I asked seller what switches it was, it took him a week to reply. By then I had pulled a key cap and checked it myself. I thought of returning it, but thought of packing it up, paying to send it back. For $38 I kept it. It is flawed but useable.

I grew up going to Vegas. Only the under 21 version, but I’ve seen enough shows to know what good looks like. I just caught Le Reve at Wynn, and it was decent, but not amazing. I think it’s even a little bit boring. But the good is that it’s a circular stage. So from pretty much any seat, you have a good view. And some of the acts are really good. The strength act, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes. But it’s a lot of Cirque du Soleil. If you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen pretty much the same things. And it’s a bit more obvious with Cirque. But the issue is I don’t know what the story is. Is it a dream? Is it a guy? Is it water? It’s just pretty pictures. I don’t know what they’re trying to say. And there’s just too much. Too many people, too many things, too many wow factors. It’s like the classic Vegas show. The more the better. So they’ve just thrown everything in. So it’s a lot. But a more restrained show would be much better. So I wouldn’t go again. It was just okay. Maybe just below okay. But I wouldn’t pay for it. A couple of my friends said they enjoyed it. If you haven’t seen it, it’s not bad. But I don’t think anyone was blown away by it. But it’s pretty average. And I think if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, you can get it for $99 instead of $125. So it’s a good deal. But I wouldn’t see it again. So if you haven’t seen it, it’s worth it. But I wouldn’t pay for it a second time.

It was 3:40 am and she found the book again, left by the flour bin near the back door. It was a library book called A Field Guide to Night Birds from Eastgate branch, and the plastic cover was cold. This was the fourth Thursday in a row she had found it. Every week she had put it in the return box on her way home and then every Thursday it turned out to be checked out again. She scraped the dough off her knuckles and opened it. There was an index card folded on the page about barn owls, with a pencil checkmark next to call. It said a long harsh scream. The card read, you leave the vent fan on, the alley smells like bread until 5am, I walk my mother's dog at 3:30 because she can't anymore, I heard one of these behind the dumpster. I keep checking this out again. Signed R. Marisol read it twice while the oven timer ticked down. Outside, the fan rattled and threw steam over the wet lid of the dumpster. She turned the card over and with a greasy pencil she used to mark the trays, wrote, rye is out at 4:15. Then she wrapped yesterday's heel in wax paper and put it on the outdoor step. Put the book on top of it and propped the back door open just an inch.
